title: How to Setup and Configure ASP.NET Core Identity
description: Set up ASP.NET Core Identity for user management with EF Core.

data.text: **ASP.NET Core Identity** is a full membership system that handles user registration, login, password hashing, role management, claims, and token generation out of the box. It uses Entity Framework Core to persist data to SQL Server by default.

terms.definition: The base class representing a user. Stores username, email, password hash, phone number, security stamp, and concurrency stamp.
Represents a named role (e.g. Admin, Manager) that users can be assigned to.
EF Core DbContext that creates the Identity schema — AspNetUsers, AspNetRoles, AspNetUserRoles, AspNetClaims, AspNetUserLogins, AspNetUserTokens, AspNetRoleClaims.
Code-first tooling that generates SQL to create or update the database schema from your C# model classes.

data.text: Three packages are needed. Install them via NuGet Package Manager or the dotnet CLI:
Create an AppUser.cs class that inherits from IdentityUser. Leave it empty for now — IdentityUser already provides Id, UserName, Email, PasswordHash, PhoneNumber, SecurityStamp, and more.

data.title: AppUser.cs

rows: The login name for the user.
Hashed password — never stored in plain text.
Regenerated whenever credentials change; invalidates old cookies.

data.text: Create AppIdentityDbContext.cs inheriting from IdentityDbContext<AppUser>. It does not need any extra code unless you want to add DbSet properties for other entities.

data.title: AppIdentityDbContext.cs

data.text: Add a ConnectionStrings section to appsettings.json. This example uses LocalDB; replace the server name for a full SQL Server instance.
Register AppIdentityDbContext and Identity in Program.cs. The AddIdentity() call wires up the user store, role store, and default token providers in one fluent chain.

data.title: Program.cs — full configuration
Middleware Order
data.text: UseAuthentication() and UseAuthorization() must come after UseRouting() and before MapControllerRoute(). If you swap them, authorization will not work correctly.
Migrations generate the SQL that creates the Identity schema. Run these commands from the project directory in Package Manager Console (PMC) or the dotnet CLI.

data.title: Create and apply migrations (dotnet CLI)
data.code:
dotnet ef migrations add InitialIdentity
dotnet ef database update

data.caption: Steps to set up ASP.NET Core Identity
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Create AppUser class] --> B[Create AppIdentityDbContext]
    B --> C[Add connection string to appsettings.json]
    C --> D[Register DbContext + Identity in Program.cs]
    D --> E[Run EF Core Migrations]
    E --> F[Identity database created with 8 tables]
    F --> G[Add authentication/authorization middleware]
    G --> H[Ready to register and sign in users]

data.text: After running migrations, the Identity database contains eight tables:

rows: Join table linking users to roles.
External login provider associations per user.
Tokens for password reset, email confirmation, 2FA.
Tracks which migrations have been applied.

data.title: Exercise: Set Up Identity from Scratch
data.description: Create a brand-new ASP.NET Core MVC project and wire up Identity end to end.
steps: Create a new ASP.NET Core MVC project.
Install the three required NuGet packages.
Add the DefaultConnection string to appsettings.json.
Run migrations and verify the IdentityDB database and its 8 tables exist.
data.expectedOutcome: Identity is fully configured. The AspNetUsers and AspNetRoles tables are present in the database and ready to store accounts.

items.text: UseAuthentication() and UseAuthorization() in the pipeline

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Identity bundles user management, password hashing, and cookie authentication.
IdentityDbContext<TUser> creates the full Identity schema via migrations.
AddIdentity<TUser, TRole>() registers all required services in one call.
The Identity database has exactly 8 tables after the initial migration.
data.takeaway: With Identity configured, you can now create users, manage roles, and add authentication to your app. Next up: implementing cookie authentication in detail.
